NAIROBI, KENYA | THE INDEPENDENT | “Lights, Camera, Empowerment: Celebrating Women in Film for International Women’s Month” As the world celebrates International Women’s Day this month, the film and television industry is revealing itself as a powerful arena of gender transformation, and a highly effected vehicle for empowering women.
This especially the case in Africa, where women occupy several leadership roles in the industry.
These roles are pivotal, as they set the tone for the sector at large, influencing the content being created, as well as the attitudes of the young audiences exposed to the material being created by the continent’s next generation of young filmmakers.
This industry’s transformed leadership is well positioned to accelerate action even further and to continue building a creative industry where women feel free to express themselves and their views of the continent and its culture.
In the vanguard of this trend is the MultiChoice Talent Factory (MTF) a pan-African network of training institutions training the next generation of African filmmakers. With training academies in Lusaka, Zambia, as well as Lagos, Nigeria and Nairobi, Kenya, the MTF provides fully paid, year-long courses in the fundamentals of film and TV production, with women well represented in every cohort.
Not only do women make up a high proportion of each year’s class, but they also win accolades in prominent film festivals as well as seeing their works premiering on major content platforms.
Most recently, Everything Light Touches – co-directed by woman MTF West Africa Academy graduate Elma Baisie – premiered on the Africa Magic Showcase channel. In East Africa, woman director Lynn Gitau – an MTV East Africa Academy graduate – partnered to create Somewhere in Kole, which premiered on the Maisha Magic Plus channel.
In every one of the MTF Africa territories, academy directors actively work to empower young woman filmmakers.
“We promote women filmmakers in numbers and in terms of creative support,” says MTF Southern Africa Academy director Chris Puta. “Women students consistently make up around 50% of our cohort intake. But I believe what is most important is that they are given license to express themselves as writers, directors and producers. This is how women’s voices enter the mainstream.”
“We believe in empowering women in the film industry through training, mentorship, and opportunities,” says MTF West Africa Academy Director Atinuke Babatunde. “We give them all the skills they require to make a statement in the industry. And that is exactly what they are doing.”
Proof of this is the recognition MTF women alumni are earning on the film festival circuit. MTF West Africa graduate and producer-director Adeola Andrea Peregrino won first prize at the LEAP Africa USAID Film contest, and second prize at the IOM Film Contest for her film Poached, as well as being selected for the Africa International Film Festival, and as a finalist at the Edo State Festival.
“MTF is committed to seeing women pursue careers in film and TV,” says MTF Academy East Director Victoria Goro. “Besides upskilling young women filmmakers, we believe a highly effective way to encourage girls and young women to get into film is to inspire them by seeing great work by young women.”
Shining examples of this inspirational work are the achievements of East Africa MTF graduate Doreen Kilimbe’s film Midnight Bride, which won Best East African Film at the Uganda Film Festival, the Audience
Award at Zambia’s Sotambe Film Festival, Best International Award at the Kalasha Film and TV Awards, and Best Actress at the Zanzibar International Film Festival.
Also making an impact was MTF Southern Africa Academy alumnus Tekla Nakale, won the best scriptwriting award for the film Ataman at the Multichoice Namibia Film Festival.
African women filmmakers are also taking charge of their own destiny in the industry by becoming involved in industry forums and even rising to leadership roles. In Namibia, MTF graduate Esther Beukes was recently appointed as Chairperson of the Board for the Namibia Film Commission.
In Botswana, former MTF student Serena Mmifinyane took time off from her work as a creative director at TV and film company N&M Productions to establish the Women in Film Guild Botswana, which is affiliated with Women in Film & TV International (WIFTI). In 2022, she was voted onto the WIFTI Board of Directors, and in 2023 became secretary of the global organisation.
“I am proud of what I have been able to achieve in the film sector,” said Mmfinyane. “But the hundreds of other young women who have come through MTF Academies have all made great strides in our industry.
Their achievements exemplify the talent and drive of Africa’s women filmmakers, and how training can be a catalyst to accelerate gender empowerment across our continent.”

a5847.t:
The Acting Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Athletics Association (GAA), Ahmed Baffoe, has announced plans to put Ghanaian athletes based in the United States into training camps ahead of the World Athletics Championship scheduled for September.
At the Ghana Athletics Open Championship held at the University of Ghana Stadium last Saturday, Mr Baffoe emphasised the importance of keeping the athletes active during the off-season.
He noted that the outdoor athletics season in the U.S. concludes in May, leaving a competitive void until the global championship in September.
“We have a little bit of an issue,” Baffoe stated. “Athletes based in the U.S., right after the outdoor competition which ends in May, wouldn’t have competitions until September. So between May and September, what do we do for these athletes? We want to try and put them in training camps.”
He proposed that these athletes be sent to Europe, where numerous athletics competitions take place during the summer to allow them to remain in peak condition.
“There are a lot of competitions coming up in Europe,” he said. “We can also help by putting them in these training camps and competitions so that it would fine-tune their performance. By the time they hit September, they’ll be at top level and perform well. Trust me, if we continue that way, we’ll win laurels at the World Championship in Tokyo.”
Baffoe expressed optimism that more Ghanaian athletes, particularly those based abroad, will qualify for individual events in addition to the relays.
“What we are hoping for is to get more athletes to qualify for the individual races — that is the 100m, 200m, 400m, and even the long-distance events. We hope that the athletes who live abroad are going to improve their performances,” he said.
The GAA boss also pointed out that while Ghana’s relay team has already qualified for the World Championship, there are other strong contenders yet to be seen on the competitive stage.
“Remember that the quartet that qualified for the World Cup are not the only strong sprinters we have. There are others such as Saminu, Azamati, and Botsio who were not able to make it for the competition,” he concluded.

Ceci du 22 au 31 août, ont annoncé les organisateurs, au cours d’une conférence de presse dans les locaux du ministère de tutelle. Par cette sortie, ils entendent lever le voile sur les grandes articulations du plus grand rendez-vous artisanal au Bénin. Sotima Michel Yotto, directeur adjoint de cabinet du ministre des petites et moyennes entreprises et de la promotion de l’emploi, Cossi Clétus Nestor Guézo, directeur général du Fonds de développement de l’artisanat et Cyr Davodoun, secrétaire général par intérim de la Chambre des métiers de l’artisanat ont, à l’occasion, dévoilé l’essentiel à retenir de cette édition.
Avec le Royaume du Maroc comme pays invité d’honneur, cette édition veut marquer un tournant décisif pour l’artisanat béninois. Le thème retenu, « Artisanat béninois : défis et enjeux de la labellisation et de la certification des produits artisanaux pour la facilitation de leur écoulement sur les marchés locaux et internationaux », traduit l’ambition de hisser le savoir-faire national aux standards internationaux. Le Snab 2025 accueillera 150 stands, dont 120 nationaux et 20 étrangers. Il entend offrir une plateforme d’échanges commerciaux et de partenariats stratégiques. Les visiteurs, béninois comme étrangers, auront accès gratuitement à une diversité de produits, à des démonstrations en direct et à des ateliers pratiques. Au-delà de sa portée nationale, le Snab se positionne désormais comme une vitrine africaine et internationale de l’artisanat. Il contribue à la diplomatie culturelle et économique du Bénin en renforçant la coopération régionale et internationale dans le secteur.
La labellisation comme enjeu stratégique
Pour les organisateurs, cette 19ᵉ édition doit laisser une empreinte durable. « La labellisation et la
certification ne sont pas un luxe, mais une clé pour propulser l’artisanat
béninois sur les grands marchés, protéger notre patrimoine et améliorer les
revenus de nos artisans. Investir dans la qualité, c’est investir dans l’avenir
», affirment-ils. Au programme, trois panels thématiques sur la labellisation
et la certification, l’exportation vers les marchés internationaux et la
digitalisation des métiers de l’artisanat. Il est aussi prévu des ateliers
pratiques et master class, un concours jeunes artisans, des animations
culturelles chaque soir et un studio Radio-TV pour une couverture en direct,
sans oublier les prix aux meilleurs artisans retenus par le jury mis en place à
cet effet. 
Quand vous y serez, et les organisateurs le recommandent
vivement, vous circulerez du bois noble à une céramique fine, d'un textile
tissé à la main à une maroquinerie méticuleuse. « Pour les bonnes affaires, nous
exposons et vendons sur place et sur commande. Beaucoup sont déjà digitalisés,
catalogues, contacts et suivis via messagerie, ce qui facilite les rachats
après ». Plus qu’un salon, le Snab se veut un vrai festival de savoir-faire. À
quelques jours de l’ouverture, l’appel est lancé au grand public, aux
institutions et aux partenaires pour se mobiliser, valoriser et célébrer
l’artisanat béninois dans toute sa diversité.
« Nous vous garantissons que vous allez avoir des
produits vraiment très intéressants. Et ne ratez pas cette occasion de vous
procurer des produits authentiquement béninois », a indiqué le secrétaire
général de la Chambre des métiers de l'artisanat. Le salon entend donner de
l'élan aux créateurs, soutient le directeur adjoint de cabinet. « Notre
objectif est de transformer l’émotion du public en commande et la commande en
emploi », ajoute le directeur du Fonds. « Venez voir comment on transforme la
matière en beauté et l'idée en métier. Repartez avec une pièce qui a une
histoire, un cadeau pour la rentrée ou un contrat d'artisan que vous ferez
travailler demain », invite-t-il par ailleurs.

La Nation Benin...

The esplanade of the Palais des Congres in Cotonou will vibrate to the rhythm of craft creativity and innovation from 22 to 31 August. The 19th edition of Benin's National Crafts Fair (Snab) promises to be a major event, held under the banner of quality, competitiveness and openness to regional and international markets.

Everything is ready as regards preparations for the 19th edition of the National Crafts Fair of Benin (Snab). For ten days, Cotonou will celebrate the excellence and creative boldness of its artisans. This will run from 22 to 31 August, the organisers announced at a press conference held at the premises of the supervising ministry. With this appearance they intended to lift the veil on the main features of the biggest craft event in Benin. Sotima Michel Yotto, deputy chief of staff to the Minister of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises and Employment Promotion, Cossi Cletus Nestor Guezo, director general of the Crafts Development Fund, and Cyr Davodoun, acting secretary general of the Chamber of Trades and Crafts, unveiled on that occasion the essentials of this edition.

With the Kingdom of Morocco as guest of honour country, this edition aims to mark a decisive turning point for Beninese crafts. The chosen theme, "Beninese crafts: challenges and stakes of the labelling and certification of craft products to facilitate their sale on local and international markets", reflects the ambition of raising national know-how to international standards. Snab 2025 will host 150 stands, 120 of them national and 20 foreign. It intends to offer a platform for commercial exchange and strategic partnerships. Visitors, Beninese and foreign alike, will have free access to a diversity of products, live demonstrations and practical workshops. Beyond its national reach, Snab now positions itself as an African and international showcase for craftsmanship. It contributes to Benin's cultural and economic diplomacy by strengthening regional and international cooperation in the sector.

Labelling as a strategic issue

For the organisers, this 19th edition must leave a lasting mark. "Labelling and certification are not a luxury, but a key to propelling Beninese crafts onto the big markets, protecting our heritage and improving the incomes of our artisans. Investing in quality is investing in the future," they affirm. On the programme are three thematic panels on labelling and certification, on exporting to international markets, and on the digitalisation of craft trades. Also planned are practical workshops and master classes, a young artisans' competition, cultural entertainment every evening and a Radio-TV studio for live coverage, not to mention prizes for the best artisans selected by the jury set up for that purpose.

When you are there - and the organisers strongly recommend it - you will move from noble wood to fine ceramics, from hand-woven textiles to meticulous leatherwork. "For good deals, we exhibit and sell on site and to order. Many are already digitalised - catalogues, contacts and follow-up via messaging, which makes repeat purchases easier." More than a fair, Snab aims to be a true festival of know-how. A few days before the opening, the call goes out to the general public, to institutions and to partners to mobilise, promote and celebrate Beninese craftsmanship in all its diversity.

"We guarantee that you will find truly very interesting products. And do not miss this opportunity to obtain authentically Beninese products," said the secretary general of the Chamber of Trades and Crafts. The fair intends to give momentum to creators, maintains the deputy chief of staff. "Our objective is to turn the public's emotion into an order, and the order into a job," adds the director of the Fund. "Come and see how we transform material into beauty and an idea into a trade. Leave with a piece that has a story, a gift for the new school year, or a craftsman's contract that will give someone work tomorrow," he further invites.

Herbs and spices are important commodities for different reasons. Not only do they serve as a very good source of income for farmers and the nation, but they are important substances for use in food spices and condiments production and medical/pharmaceutical industries.
Consequently, farming herbs or spices can be an excellent investment opportunity for Nigerians both young and retired.
Herbs are generally identified as the leaves of non-woody plants that are used as an aromatic supplement.
Spices, on the other hand, comes from the roots, fruits, seeds, rhizomes, stems, leaves, bark, and flowers.
Herbs are usually fresh or dried, chopped, or whole. Spices are usually dried and take many forms such as crushed or ground to a powder.
With the growing population and demand for supplement and alternative medical approach in curing illness, the demand for aromatic organic herbs and spices will continue to grow alongside food production such as grains, fruits and vegetables.
Nigeria is a leading producer of many popular Herbs and spices has gone beyond such as ginger, turmeric, pepper, and nutmeg, uda, uziza, scent leaves, lemon grass, neem which Nigeria is a leading producer, we have in high demand aromatic organic herbs such as Artemesia, lavender, marjoram, Rosemary, Variegated oregano, king of bitters, Dill, Choco mint, Mint leave, Sweet basil .
According to the National Bureau of Statistics, the herbs and spice market in Nigeria is valued at over N100 billion, with ginger being the most valuable spice.
The country is also the world’s second-largest producer of ginger after India.
Additionally, Nigeria is the third-largest producer of turmeric, with an annual production of 20,000 metric tons.
The global demand for herbs and spices is increasing, with the spice market expected to reach $22.8 billion by 2026.
The increasing popularity of ethnic and healthy foods is a major driver of the global herbs and spice market.
Nigeria has a great potential for herbs and spice farming due to the suitable climate and soil for growing spices.
Herbs and Spice farming in Nigeria presents a great opportunity for export, as the herbs and spices produced in the country are in high demand globally.
The export market for herbs and spices is growing, with Europe and North America being the major importers of herbs and spices.
Nigeria’s ginger is exported to several countries, including the United States, Japan, and the United Kingdom.
The local market is sure as most herbs and spices are imported.
Growing herbs and spices in Nigeria is a hidden opportunity, Due to the multiple uses these plants, herbs and spices have been a successful economic investment for many growers.
Spice has proven itself as a lucrative business. Saffron Artemesia, Rosemary and scorpion tail for instance, remains more expensive than gold, despite the opportunity that farming with these botanicals have, Nigeria still produces less than 5% of these herbs and spices worldwide.
What Is Herbs And Spice
Herbs and Spice farming refers to the cultivation, harvesting, processing, and marketing of various spices and herbs used for culinary, medicinal, and cosmetic purposes.
Spices are plants or plant parts that have aromatic properties and are used to add flavor, fragrance, and color to food, beverages, and other products.
Spice farming involves growing a variety of herbs and plants such as ginger, turmeric, garlic, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, black pepper, Artemesia, lavender, marjoram, Rosemary, Variegated oregano, king of bitters, Dill, Choco mint, Mint leave, Sweet basil and many others.
These plants require special conditions to grow and thrive, including specific soils, temperatures, and humidity levels. Once harvested, the herbs and spices must be carefully processed, dried, and packaged to maintain their quality and potency.
Herbs and Spice farming is an essential industry in Nigeria , where spices are used widely in local cuisines and traditional medicine.
Moreover, the increasing demand for herbs and spices globally presents a significant opportunity for farmers in Nigeria and Africa to expand their business and earn valuable foreign exchange by exporting their products.
Benefits Of Spice Farming In Nigeria
• High demand: Spice farming is a profitable venture due to the high demand for spices both locally and internationally.
Spices are used in the food and beverage industry, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and other industries.
• Diversification: Herbs and Spice farming allows farmers to diversify their agricultural production, which reduces risk and ensures steady income.
• Economic development: The herbs and spice industry has the potential to contribute significantly to the economic development of Nigeria and Africa by creating job opportunities, increasing exports, and boosting foreign exchange earnings.
• Health benefits: Spices are known for their medicinal properties and are used in traditional medicine to treat various ailments.
Incorporating spices in the diet has been linked to numerous health benefits, such as reducing inflammation, improving digestion, and boosting immunity.
• Environmental benefits: It can have positive environmental impacts, including soil conservation, carbon sequestration, and promoting biodiversity.
• Cultural preservation: Spices have a cultural and historical significance, and their farming helps preserve traditional knowledge and practices.
• Flavor enhancement: are used to enhance the flavor and aroma of food, which can lead to increased consumption and sales.
• Export potential: Nigeria has a high potential to export spices to other countries, especially in the European Union and the United States, which import large quantities of spices.
• Income generation: Farming herbs and spice can generate significant income for farmers, especially when grown on a large scale and marketed effectively.
• Value addition: Herbs and Spices can be processed into various products such as essential oils, powder, and capsules, which increases their value and can lead to higher profits for farmers.

ABUJA – USAID Nigeria-State Accountability, Transparency, and Effectiveness (‘State2State’) Activity has called on the States in Nigeria to prioritise sustainable reforms to promote good governance in Nigeria.
The State2State made the call at the National Conference for State Transformation Committees (STCs) held in Abuja.
In an interview with newsmen, the Senior Governance Advisor of The Foreign CommonWealth and Development Office (FCDO), Chris Okeke, tasked States across the country to embrace good practices and approaches to sustain reforms beyond programme support, political transitions and changes to office holders.
Okeke also urged states to focus attention on inclusivity, youth empowerment and public service reforms to improve productivity in governance.
He underscored the need for public sector reforms that would streamline bureaucratic procedures and improve transparency and accountability in governance systems.
He also pointed out the indispensable role of the civil service in driving sustainable reforms in governance.
According to him, “The important thing for the long-term sustenance of reforms is the issue of bureaucracy and how the civil service can contribute to the sustainability of reforms, including reforms such as public financial management systems, public service reforms, empowerment and accountability.
“During our discussion, we highlighted the critical point with regard to the suitability of the public service structure.
“We questioned whether it was fit for purpose, considering the functions and human skills within the civil service.
“Additionally, we examined how effective the planning and preparation of key talents were, as well as the issue of succession gaps within the civil service.”
Okeke stressed the need for state governments to focus on developing local capacity to effectively manage the resources that have already been provided.
Also speaking, a Senior Public Financial Management Expert, Dr. Uzochukwu Amakom, emphasised the need for institutions to adopt good practices that conform to global standards to achieve their set goals and objectives.
He said: “Whether you are doing reforms or not, the end point is how does it affect service delivery?
“It is not creating new institutions that matter, it is the result. This is what reforms entail.
“If you do good realistic revenue forecasting, you embrace good cash planning and expenditure prioritisation, there will be good results.”
Amakom, therefore, urged states to insist on planning realistic budgets and revenue, which is a crucial step to ensuring that Nigeria’s resources are prudently managed.
According to him, “It is vital for states to prioritise accountability and transparency while planning their budgets to ensure that funds are allocated to the areas that need them the most.”

HIV response researchers have sounded the alarm over recent global funding cuts, saying they have severely disrupted efforts to combat HIV, threatening life-saving research, prevention and treatment.
The experts addressed the press ahead of the 13th International Aids Society (IAS 2025) Conference, taking place in Kigali, Rwanda and virtually from July 13 to 17.
They presented scientific highlights from four studies selected from abstracts being showcased at the conference.
During the conference, the experts revealed predictive modelling and real-world data from Africa and Latin America, indicating rising HIV acquisitions, stalled treatment and fragile health systems.
IAS president Dr Beatriz Grinsztejn said that, on one hand, the world is witnessing extraordinary scientific breakthroughs that could transform prevention and treatment and “even bring us closer to a cure”.
- Advertisement -
“On the other hand, these very advances are under threat from massive funding cuts that risk stalling clinical trials, slowing our progress and jeopardising the achievements we’ve fought so hard to attain,” Dr Grinsztejn said.
IAS president-elect Professor Kenneth Ngure said that the sudden cuts to United States (US) funding, announced earlier this year, have been “deeply felt” across the African continent by millions of people who rely on HIV prevention, testing and treatment services.
HIV incidence and related deaths are expected to rise significantly in sub-Saharan Africa due to disruptions in funding for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) under the US President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar).
This is according to a preprint modelling study presented by lead author Dr Jack Stone, Associate Professor in Infectious Disease Mathematical Modelling at the University of Bristol.
- Advertisement -
- Advertisement -
By late 2024, PrEP funded by Pepfar had been accessed by nearly 700,000 people across 28 sub-Saharan African countries, including Malawi, before funding for the medication was paused in January 2025.
The study suggests that this pause could result in approximately 6,671 additional HIV acquisitions over one year, and a further 3,617 cases over the subsequent five years.
More than 2,900 of these additional cases are projected to occur among gay and bisexual men who have sex with men, while over 2,000 are expected among female sex workers.
“It is crucial that funding is secured to continue and expand PrEP services in sub-Saharan Africa,” Dr Stone said.
Meanwhile, Zackie Achmat, founder of the Treatment Action Campaign and a member of the Global HIV Treatment Coalition, issued a call to action on the urgent need for debt refinancing to protect the HIV response in low- and middle-income countries.
“You can’t end the Aids pandemic while African nations must choose between paying creditors and saving lives. As someone who has lived with HIV for more than half my life, I have seen the cost of political inaction.
“We fought for treatment when the world said it was impossible. Now, the convergence of crushing debt and funding cuts threatens everything we’ve built. We need urgent debt restructuring so African countries can invest in saving lives instead of servicing debt,” Achmat said.
The IAS Conference on HIV Science is regarded as the world’s most influential meeting on HIV research and its applications.
This biennial conference presents “the critical advances in basic, clinical and operational HIV research that move science into policy and practice”.

Persistent crop failure has taught Chipakuza villagers in Chikwawa that repeating farming methods that have been tried with little profit cannot suddenly bring extraordinary results.
The farming community under Traditional Authority (T/A) Lundu has switched from rain-fed agriculture to irrigation in the wake of hunger caused by uncertainties associated with climate change.
The rural population faces one disaster to another, especially drought and flooding.
However, many rue the loss and damage caused by Cyclone Freddy in March last year. The world’s longest-running cyclone dumped floods, mudslides and strong winds that affected over 2.2 million people in the Southern Region.
A year after the torrents and floods destroyed crops and buried fields in silt, the community was hit hard by drought caused by the El Nino weather pattern across southern Africa.
Lead farmer Matias Nyazi recalls the prolonged dry spell scorching maturing crops that were expected to end hunger caused by the devastating floods.
“We looked at the data and noticed that hunger was the common problem, so we agreed to embrace irrigation farming,” he says.
Njazi’s family of four is among 126 households that collectively rented farmland near a vast sugarcane plantation for irrigation in Nchalo Estate, Chikwawa.
Illovo Sugar (Malawi) plc irrigates the vast sugarcane fields throughout the dry season, an awakening for communities that rains are not everything crops need to flourish.
Unlike many farmers in Malawi, the villagers in the vicinity are reaping the benefits of irrigation amid unpredictable rains worsened by climate change.
The farmers take turns in the irrigated fields, with the first group cultivating from March to July and the second July to November.
Njazi pays K50 000 per season for a field half the size of a football ground, where he harvests 10 to 12 bags in winter. During the rainy season, he yields less than half the winter harvest.
The farmer hires a water pump worth K30 000 per cropping season to irrigate the plot where he applies two bags of fertiliser worth about K200 000.
“The cost of irrigation is much lower than buying 50 kilogrammes of maize at K45 000. At the current price, I need K450 000 for 10 bags,” he says.
Njazi also grows vegetables that earn him at least K10 000 a week.
“I use the money to meet the daily needs of my family and boost my farming business,” he says.
T/A Lundu’s drought-prone area is among communities where the Catholic Relief Service (CRS) is implementing a community driven data collection tool to improve food security and livelihoods amid climate change.
CRS co-designed the rapid feedback monitoring system (RFMS) with Cornell University and the National Statistics Office (NSO).
The technology, funded by the US Agency for International Development (USAid), captures real-time data in communities to inform decisions.
Every month, community-based enumerators collect information from selected households to understand how their livelihoods change throughout the year.
The data collectors share their findings with community members for collective learning, validation and decision-making. They also share the insights with government and development partners.
CRS plans to launch a dashboard where users can access essential information for every district and probably T/A at a click of a few buttons.
They envisage the tool putting vital indicators at the fingertip of anyone who wants them, streamlining community development interventions.
According to Group village head (GVH) Chipakuza, the findings have ranked food insecurity as a major concern for 92 percent of the households in the area.
“Based on the reports, as community leaders, we had to think of what we can do to end hunger. We met and identified this irrigated piece of land for communal use to sustain our families,” the traditional leader recalls.
The community also used the data to persuade development partners who constructed a dyke to prevent flooding, which disrupts schooling and livelihoods in the community.
“We use the same data to convince well-wishers to help us,” says GVH Chipakuza.
The data sheets with simplified visual aids to break down and illustrate the big numbers come in Chichewa, the widely spoken local language, for easy understanding.
Area Development Committee (ADC) vice-chairperson Evelyn Jonasi says the RFMS has made decision-making simple.
“When the ADC wants to present issues to the council or lobby for project funding, we use this data as our backing. With data, it has really become easy for the council and other development partners to assist our communities,” he states.
The World Bank rates RFMS highly as a cost- effective and reliable tool for capturing real-time data relating to poverty and climate change.
CRS trained 300 community-based enumerators who have been using smartphones to capture information from selected households since 2020.
The system uses machine learning to predict future outcomes such as households likely to be affected by flooding and areas that would recover quickly.
This paves the way for life-saving decisions, from effective planning and risk reduction to disaster response.

"Un cessez-le-feu à ce stade ci ne bénéficierait qu'au Hamas", a déclaré mardi à la presse le porte-parole du Conseil de sécurité nationale de la Maison-Blanche, John Kirby, qui a aussi prévenu que la situation allait encore empirer pour les civils. Si Washington s'oppose à un cessez-le-feu complet, des arrêts sporadiques dans les combats afin de faciliter l'acheminement de l'aide à la bande de Gaza doivent être "considérés", a-t-il nuancé. "Nous voulons voir les mesures de protection pour les civils. Or des pauses dans les opérations sont un outil, une tactique, qui peuvent y parvenir pour une période temporaire (...) mais cela n'est pas la même chose qu'un cessez-le-feu", a-t-il ajouté. 
                                 
                                                                                                                                                
                                    Une aide humanitaire "pas assez rapide"
Le président américain Joe Biden a estimé mardi que l'aide humanitaire n'arrivait pas assez vite dans la bande de Gaza, assiégée et pilonnée sans relâche par Israël depuis l'attaque sanglante du Hamas le 7 octobre. L'acheminement n'est "pas assez rapide", a déclaré le président américain, questionné par la presse à la Maison-Blanche sur l'aide humanitaire, qui a commencé à entrer samedi, mais au compte-gouttes, dans ce territoire de 362 km2 où s'entassent 2,4 millions de Palestiniens. Dans ce contexte, le secrétaire général de l'Onu Antonio Guterres a appelé à un "cessez-le-feu humanitaire immédiat" entre Israël et le mouvement islamiste palestinien Hamas. "Pour apaiser cette souffrance immense, faciliter la distribution de l'aide de façon plus sûre, et faciliter la libération des otages, je répète mon appel à un cessez-le-feu humanitaire immédiat", a déclaré au siège de l'Onu M. Guterres, en dénonçant des "violations claires" du droit humanitaire à Gaza. "Monsieur le secrétaire général, dans quel monde vivez vous", a lancé le ministre israélien des Affaires étrangères Eli Cohen avant d'annuler sa rencontre avec Antonio Guterres. "Comment pouvez-vous conclure un accord de cessez-le-feu avec quelqu'un qui a juré de tuer et de détruire votre propre existence", a ajouté Eli Cohen face à cette demande de "cessez-le-feu humanitaire immédiat". Le ministère de la Santé du Hamas affirme que 5 791 personnes ont été tuées depuis le 7 octobre et le début des frappes israéliennes sur la bande de Gaza. Ces bombardements sont une riposte à l'attaque sans précédent menée ce jour-là par le Hamas et qui a fait plus de 1 400 morts, tandis que plus de 200 personnes sont retenues en otage.
a7036.en:
United States: The White House repeats that a ceasefire in Gaza “would only benefit Hamas”

“A ceasefire at this stage would only benefit Hamas,” the spokesman for the White House National Security Council, John Kirby, told the press on Tuesday, also warning that the situation was going to get even worse for civilians. While Washington opposes a full ceasefire, sporadic halts in the fighting in order to facilitate the delivery of aid to the Gaza Strip should be “considered,” he qualified. “We want to see protective measures for civilians. Now, pauses in operations are a tool, a tactic, that can achieve that for a temporary period (...) but that is not the same thing as a ceasefire,” he added.

Humanitarian aid “not fast enough”

US President Joe Biden said on Tuesday that humanitarian aid was not arriving fast enough in the Gaza Strip, besieged and relentlessly pounded by Israel since Hamas's bloody attack of 7 October. The delivery is “not fast enough,” the American president said when questioned by the press at the White House about humanitarian aid, which began entering on Saturday, but only in a trickle, into this territory of 362 km2 where 2.4 million Palestinians are crowded together. In this context, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for an “immediate humanitarian ceasefire” between Israel and the Palestinian Islamist movement Hamas. “To ease this immense suffering, to make the distribution of aid safer, and to facilitate the release of the hostages, I repeat my call for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire,” Mr Guterres said at UN headquarters, while denouncing “clear violations” of humanitarian law in Gaza. “Mr Secretary-General, what world are you living in,” the Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs Eli Cohen shot back before cancelling his meeting with Antonio Guterres. “How can you conclude a ceasefire agreement with someone who has sworn to kill and destroy your very existence,” Eli Cohen added in response to this call for an “immediate humanitarian ceasefire.” Hamas's Health Ministry states that 5,791 people have been killed since 7 October and the beginning of the Israeli strikes on the Gaza Strip. These bombardments are a response to the unprecedented attack carried out that day by Hamas, which left more than 1,400 dead, while more than 200 people are being held hostage.

NYT: les États-Unis priveront le soutien du pays, où initialement n'a pas prévu de mettre fin à l'aide
NEW YORK, 10 avril. / TASS/. L'administration du président américain Donald Trump a réduit les programmes d'aide pour plusieurs pays où elle avait initialement promis de maintenir son soutien. Cela a été rapporté par le journal The New York Times (NYT) en référence aux listes fournies aux fonctionnaires et aux travailleurs humanitaires.
Selon ces listes, les États-Unis cesseront de financer des programmes en Afghanistan, en Irak, en Jordanie, en République Démocratique du Congo, au Liban, à Madagascar, au Mali, au Niger, au Nigéria, en Syrie, en Somalie, au Tchad et au Yémen. Reuters citant des sources le 9 avril a rapporté que plus tard, la maison Blanche a décidé de rétablir les paiements dans le cadre du programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) au Liban, en Syrie, en Somalie, en Jordanie, en Irak et en Équateur.
Le PAM estime que le refus de Washington de fournir de l'aide aura le plus d'impact en Afghanistan, où environ 2 millions de personnes, dont 400 000 enfants, dépendent de la nourriture. La population du Yémen souffrira également, où 2,4 millions de personnes reçoivent de la nourriture dans le cadre de programmes humanitaires.
Les interlocuteurs du NYT à l'Agence américaine pour le développement international (USAID) ont souligné qu'ils apprennent souvent la fin du prochain programme directement des organisations humanitaires qui cessent de recevoir des fonds.
Au début de février, Trump a suspendu les activités de l'USAID, qui a alloué une quantité importante de fonds pour financer des organisations internationales. Plus tard, l'administration américaine a annoncé son intention d'annuler 92% des contrats de l'agence et du département d'Etat pour aider. Le 10 mars, le secrétaire d'état américain Marco Rubio, précédemment nommé à la tête par intérim de l'USAID, a annoncé que le gouvernement américain, à l'issue d'un audit de six semaines, avait officiellement mis fin à 83% des programmes de l'agence. Selon lui, dans le cadre de 5,2 mille contrats qui ont été annulés, des dizaines de milliards de dollars ont été dépensés non pas dans l'intérêt des États - Unis, et dans certains cas-au détriment d'eux.
a7162.en:
NYT: The United States will deprive of support the country where it had initially not planned to end aid

NEW YORK, 10 April. /TASS/. The administration of American President Donald Trump has cut aid programmes for several countries where it had initially promised to maintain its support. This was reported by the newspaper The New York Times (NYT), citing lists provided to officials and humanitarian workers.

According to these lists, the United States will cease financing programmes in Afghanistan, Iraq, Jordan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Lebanon, Madagascar, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Syria, Somalia, Chad and Yemen. Reuters, citing sources on 9 April, reported that later the White House decided to restore payments under the World Food Programme (WFP) in Lebanon, Syria, Somalia, Jordan, Iraq and Ecuador.

The WFP estimates that Washington's refusal to provide aid will have the greatest impact in Afghanistan, where about 2 million people, including 400,000 children, depend on the food. The population of Yemen will also suffer, where 2.4 million people receive food under humanitarian programmes.

The NYT's interlocutors at the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) stressed that they often learn of the end of the next programme directly from the humanitarian organisations that stop receiving funds.

At the beginning of February, Trump suspended the activities of USAID, which had allocated a significant quantity of funds to finance international organisations. Later, the American administration announced its intention to cancel 92% of the aid contracts of the agency and of the State Department. On 10 March, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, previously appointed acting head of USAID, announced that the American government, at the conclusion of a six-week audit, had officially ended 83% of the agency's programmes. According to him, under the 5,200 contracts that were cancelled, tens of billions of dollars had been spent not in the interests of the United States, and in some cases to their detriment.

Harare, (New Ziana) – The Mid-Term Review of the 18th Session of the Zimbabwe-Zambia Joint Permanent Commission on Cooperation (JPCC) ended on a high note on Thursday, with senior officials from the two countries reaffirming their commitment to strengthening bilateral ties across key sectors.
The end of the senior officials meeting will lead to the meeting of Foreign Affairs Ministers from both countries later on Thursday.
Speaking at the close of the session, Zimbabwean permanent secretary for Foreign Affairs and International Trade, Albert Chimbindi hailed the meeting as notably productive, adding that it was conducted in a spirit of camaraderie befitting the excellent state of relations between the two neighbouring countries.
He expressed gratitude to his Zambian counterpart, Etambuyu Gundersen, for her effective leadership, as well as to the Zimbabwean ambassador to Zambia, Charity Charamba, and the Zambian chargé de’affaires to Zimbabwe, Nabulanga Natlasha, for their contributions to the success of the review.
Chimbindi also commended the tireless work of the sectoral committees and officials who charted the way forward during the meeting, whose deliberations covered a wide range of areas including political, diplomatic, governance, economic, trade, and socio-cultural cooperation.
He said the outcomes of the review serve as a roadmap to strengthen both bilateral and multilateral relations.
“In light of the unprecedented geopolitical developments, rising tariffs, and the decline in foreign aid that are disrupting trade and investment flows across the SADC region, it is in our national interests to optimise opportunities for mutual benefit,” he said.
He noted that both countries had set clear benchmarks and targets to ensure accountability to their principals, stressing the need for resilience and a united voice in advancing the development priorities of the Southern African region and the continent at large.
The session concluded with Ambassador Chimbindi officially handing over the outcomes of the meeting for consideration by the respective Ministers, underscoring the importance of implementing decisions that emerged from the review.
The Zimbabwe-Zambia JPCC remains a vital platform for deepening cooperation, enhancing trade and investment, and fostering stronger people-to-people ties between the two nations.
New Ziana

Les responsables de Plan International étaient face à la presse, le jeudi 10 octobre 2024, dans le cadre de la célébration de la Journée internationale des filles pour parler de la nécessaire protection de ces dernières et de leur droit à l’égalité des chances.
Le représentant Résident de Plan International Mali, Jackson Acha Atam, la nouvelle Directrice Pays de Plan International Mali, Korotoum Diarra, la nouvelle Directrice Régionale d'Afrique de l’Ouest et du Centre de Plan International, Oumou Yanogo étaient face à la presse le 11 octobre 2024, au siège de l'organisation à Sotuba Aci pour célébrer la Journée internationale des filles,  sous le thème «La vision des filles pour le futur».
Le Plan International Mali, faut-il le signaler,  a pour mission de protéger le droit des enfants, d’appeler les décideurs à plus d’engagement en faveur de l’épanouissement de la fille, de l’égalité des chances.
Initiée par la Résolution 66\170 du 19 décembre 2011 de l’Organisation des Nations-Unies, la Journée internationale des filles vise à porter une attention particulière sur la situation des filles afin de reconnaître leurs droits, identifier et corriger les obstacles qui affectent leur plein épanouissement.
Dans ce cadre, le ministère en charge de la Promotion de la femme, de l’enfant et de la famille entend relever le défi de la scolarisation des filles, en mettant un cachet particulier sur les filières scientifiques. Ainsi le thème national de la journée «La refondation de l’éducation à travers un accompagnement des filles dans les filières scientifiques», illustre parfaitement cette vision.
Dans son intervention, Mlle Korotoum Diarra a insisté sur la nécessité de promouvoir le droit des enfants et l’égalité pour les filles, particulièrement victimes des violences de tous genres, notamment dans les pays en conflits. C’est pourquoi, selon elle, le Plan International s’est fixé des objectifs pour mettre en valeur les capacités des filles en tant que leaders, tout en soulignant la nécessité d’entreprendre des efforts spécifiques pour leur autonomisation à long terme ; créer un réseau solidaire pour les filles et les jeunes femmes participantes et assurer une visibilité dans la presse et les réseaux sociaux des enjeux qu’elles défendent.
Plan International oeuvre aussi à mettre en lumière les problèmes prioritaires pour les jeunes filles dans différents et contextes et explorer comment les partenaires peuvent aider à garantir que leurs besoins soient pris en compte dans les politiques et le développement international ;et discuter de la manière dont les acteurs peuvent adopter une position encore plus active dans la promotion des filles et de leurs droits.
Pour la réalisation de ces ambitions énoncées, elle lance un appel au gouvernement, aux acteurs socio-politiques pour des actions communes en faveur du respect du droit des enfants et l’égalité des chances pour les filles. Il s’agit notamment d’arrêter et condamner toutes les violences graves contre les enfants dans les conflits ; de soutenir une éducation sûre et inclusive pour les enfants et les jeunes ; de cibler l’aide humanitaire pour l’accès des enfants à la nourriture, à l’eau et aux abris.
Oumou Yanogué a exprimé sa fierté de l’organisation de la Journée dédiée à la fille. Elle a félicité l’engagement de Plan international qui met la jeune fille au centre de ses actions dont l’éducation, la santé, pour son épanouissement.
Jackson Acha Atam, Directeur pays sortant de Plan International Mali, a rappelé le contexte de la célébration de la Journée dédiée à la fille, qui dénote, selon lui, de la particularité des besoins de la femme. Il croit en la capacité des femmes à acquérir les compétences et exercer les mêmes métiers que les hommes. Il estime que la jeune fille a besoin d’un accompagnement particulier afin qu’elle jouisse de tous ses droits. Cela, précise-t-il, passe par la sensibilisation des parents sur les conséquences du mariage précoce, de la déscolarisation des filles.
Broulaye Koné, Stagiaire

International Day of the Girl Child: Plan Mali still active for equal opportunities

The officials of Plan International met the press on Thursday 10 October 2024, as part of the celebration of the International Day of the Girl Child, to speak about the necessary protection of girls and their right to equal opportunities.

The Resident Representative of Plan International Mali, Jackson Acha Atam, the new Country Director of Plan International Mali, Korotoum Diarra, and the new Regional Director for West and Central Africa of Plan International, Oumou Yanogo, met the press on 11 October 2024 at the organisation's headquarters in Sotuba Aci to celebrate the International Day of the Girl Child, under the theme "Girls' vision for the future."

Plan International Mali, it should be noted, has the mission of protecting children's rights, of calling on decision-makers for greater commitment in favour of girls' development and equal opportunities.

Initiated by Resolution 66/170 of 19 December 2011 of the United Nations Organisation, the International Day of the Girl Child aims to give particular attention to the situation of girls in order to recognise their rights, and to identify and correct the obstacles that affect their full development.

In this context, the ministry in charge of the Promotion of Women, Children and the Family intends to take up the challenge of girls' schooling, placing a particular stamp on scientific fields. Thus the national theme of the day, "The refoundation of education through the support of girls in scientific fields," perfectly illustrates this vision.

In her remarks, Miss Korotoum Diarra insisted on the need to promote children's rights and equality for girls, who are particularly victims of violence of all kinds, notably in countries in conflict. That is why, according to her, Plan International has set itself objectives to bring out girls' capacities as leaders, while underlining the need to undertake specific efforts for their long-term empowerment; to create a solidarity network for the participating girls and young women; and to ensure visibility in the press and on social networks of the issues they defend.

Plan International also works to highlight the priority problems for young girls in different contexts and to explore how partners can help ensure that their needs are taken into account in policies and international development; and to discuss how actors can adopt an even more active position in promoting girls and their rights.

To achieve these stated ambitions, she issues an appeal to the government and to socio-political actors for joint action in favour of respect for children's rights and equal opportunities for girls. This includes in particular halting and condemning all grave violence against children in conflicts; supporting safe and inclusive education for children and young people; and targeting humanitarian aid for children's access to food, water and shelter.

Oumou Yanogue expressed her pride in the organisation of the Day dedicated to the girl child. She congratulated the commitment of Plan International, which places the young girl at the centre of its actions, including education and health, for her development.

Jackson Acha Atam, outgoing country director of Plan International Mali, recalled the context of the celebration of the Day dedicated to the girl child, which, according to him, points to the particular nature of women's needs. He believes in women's capacity to acquire the skills and practise the same trades as men. He considers that the young girl needs particular support so that she may enjoy all her rights. That, he specifies, requires raising parents' awareness of the consequences of early marriage and of girls dropping out of school.

Broulaye Kone, Intern

In 2011, the Kenyan government banned the manufacture and import of plastic bags. The intention was good: to protect against the environmental hazard that plastic bags have become. The implementation, however, was poor, and plastic bags remain an all too prominent feature of the Kenyan landscape.
An earlier ban, in 2007, on plastic bags less than 30 microns thick, failed after manufacturers and retail outlets threatened to pass on the cost of using other materials to the consumer. Politicians fought the ban amid suspicions that they benefitted financially from plastic bag manufacturers, and it was never enforced.
But civil society campaigners are renewing the fight against plastic bags in Kenya, arguing that they pose a real threat to the health of citizens. Plastic bags have been implicated in a recent outbreak of cholera, which has killed 246 people – the water-borne disease thrives in drains that are blocked by plastic bags.
For James Wakibia, an environmentalist, eliminating plastic bags is a personal war. Having lived in London estate on the outskirts of Nakuru town, right next to the Gioto dumpsite, one of the biggest in the country, Wakibia watched a plastic bag mountain be created in front of him.
In 2013, he felt he had to take action. After the establishment of the county government (following Kenya’s devolution process), Wakibia collected 10,000 signatures seeking the relocation of the dumpsite.
“We held a meeting with the Chief Officer of Environment, Richard Rop, who promised that the government would use 52-million Kenyan shillings (R7.8-million) to control the garbage, with half of that amount going into fencing the dumpsite. Three years down the line, nothing has happened,” he added.
Wakibia analysed the type of garbage that was trashed in the facility, and realised that it was mostly plastic bags. “I knew if I had to solve the crisis I needed to deal with the small plastic paper bags, popularly known as the single use bags, that flew everywhere,” he said.
His frustration increased when he came across a report saying that 20 thousand tonnes of garbage are collected in Lake Nakuru, one of Kenya’s largest water sources, every year. He believes this garbage is responsible for the rise in water levels in the Lake, which is threatening local homes and livelihoods.
Wakibia looked around the country to see how other Kenyan counties dealt with the problem.
“Nairobi County had admitted that 70 percent of the garbage collected was [plastic] bags. Lamu, Malindi and Kisii and had also indicated that they would deal with the issue,” he said.
Nairobi’s local assembly is contemplating the Nairobi City County Plastic Carry Bags Control Bill (2014), lodged by Nairobi County Assembly representative Abdi Hassan Guyo, and seeks to ban recycled, nonbiodegradable plastic bags and containers from virgin plastic less than 30 microns thick and 20cm by 30cm in size.
In December 2015, Wakibia presented another 10,000 signatures to Nakuru County Clerk Joseph Malinda, which called for the total ban of plastics below 100 microns. Nakuru county legislature is considering the petition, and has sent a team to Gioto dumpsite to assess the severity of the problem.
Naturally, there is fierce opposition to all proposed bans from plastic bag manufacturers. Githinji Kinyanjui, the managing director of Cocorico Investment, a polythene manufacturing firm in Nairobi, challenged the government to come up with a better way of cleaning up the plastic bags mess.
“There should be separate bags for different garbage in the homes. Our challenge is when we mix bags and other dirty garbage. We actually have a shortage of clean polythene bags for recycling,” says Kinyanjui. He said it is impossible to ban the bags, saying that the high demand for them is market driven.
Nakuru County Speaker Susan Kihika called for the enforcement of the law passed in 2007 that would see the total eradication of small plastic bags in the country.
“When we control plastic bags menace we immediately deal with issues like water borne diseases including cholera and dysentery which are basically as a result of blocked and clogged drainage in the county,” said Kihika.
Along with governments, Wakibia believes that businesses can play a vital role in fixing the problem.
“Supermarkets are the biggest producers of plastics, with an estimated one million bags behind distributed in the country annually. Unfortunately they do not follow up on where the bags end up and hence they are the biggest culprits in the environmental degradation. They should be the ones on the forefront in creating awareness and running environmental campaigns,” he said, proposing that supermarkets introduce customer reward points for people who use recyclable bags instead.
Environmentalist Emily Kimani said that the easiest way to curb the menace was to create a regulation to bar their manufacture.
“Currently we do not have better mechanisms to control their spread in the country and the only way to do so is to completely stop their manufacture,” she said. DM
Njeri Kimani is a journalist based in Nakuru, Kenya.
